title: Blues, Ellington's rhythm and why dancers took taps off
summary: Green says Ellington's East St. Louis Toodle-oo gave the blues a beat, clubs like the Cotton Club moved downtown, and dancers took off their taps for lack of choreography.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: You were talking before about the different type of music that was going on at the same time. Can you tell me a little bit more about that and how it affected the tap dancers?

Yeah, well they was really trying to save the blues, you see, the blues was getting unpopular. See, because they wanted to kind of reject the blues, because the tempo of the blues, they hadn't quite came to the applying tempo, like a beat, see -- blues was more like a ballad. See? On some say it's kind of meditative. Blues. You see, until like Pop -- Ruff Ellington's brother, I mean he -- he did East St. Louis Toodle-oo. And that gave the blues a beat, you see. Someway up here in Columbus Circle there, I think he and Sonny Greer and -- I think Harry Carnegie and Johnny Hodges, you know, and Cootie Williams, Tricky Sam, you know, they was all -- I called them doctors of music because they were so overwhelming, you see. And, there's no way for you not to catch a feeling, I mean, when they'd start like that. I think he retitled that Sitting and Rocking, I think he retitled East St. Louise Toodle-oo. And he was cited by the composer, which was another pop, W. C. Handy. So, this guy, he became very popular, think it was named Rayburn, something -- Ross Rayburn, something like that. He had a -- he had a jazz band, you know, but they played like house music, what they called house music and they would intro-

duce these new works by the composers from ASCAP's, you see, and the off-Broadway shows, like this thing, what was it? It was some (unintelligible) -- think they turned that out too, LEW Leslie and his partner, there. He had a partner, you see? And -- that was the darn -- name of the darned show, I think it was Zanzibar, something. It was called. And, which after those times, I mean, they was going to rename these clubs.

You see the Cotton Club people were going to reinstate themselves, you know, relocated, like they was gonna come down like right on Broadway, right into the -- right into the detail, the degree of it all, you see? And --
In other words, places like the Cotton Club, the Elks Rendezvous -- the Savoy Ballroom, were closing down, is that correct? And they want to sort of popularize tap dance now, back on Broadway?

Yeah, well tap dance never did get unpopular. You see, it just got anaemic, see? The people took their taps off, you see? And that was just -- I guess you would say like some bird leave a nest in a tree somewhere and then they never know when the tree will have that bird again, in the nest, you see, and that -- had to be something else by the time the flock gets back.
Why did they take the taps off the shoes?
: Why was -- any particular reason? You say they took the taps off the shoes?

Yes, quite a number of them did, because they didn't have enough choreography -- that's really waht it was. See? They had a-- like what we would call a professor of music, physicist is to science, you see -- even playwrights, they were unknowns -- you see? And people wanted to -- they wanted to get in musicals, you see, and in the musicals they didn't feature a lot of tap dancing. See? It was mostly being visual.

See, like -- like I say, to get -- to get into play like table tennis is today, like you have to volley for the serve. You see? What I mean, they had this versatility, which is tap dancing, you see? In case they was asked, you know, costume departments, and so forth, they would -- they would always outfit the performers, see?
